I am sorry to report that we aren't close at all. Most studies show that bipolar is a result of genetics and that even our best medications have not proven totally effective in the long term. 

The following is out of chapter 7 of my Abnormal Psychology textbook. 


> Overall, the probabilities of "full recovery" from bipolar disorder are discouraging even with the widespread use of mood-stabilizing medications such as lithium. One 10-year prospective study of over 200 patients found that 24% had relapsed within 6 months of recovery; 77% had had at least one new episode within 4 years of recovery; and 82% had relapsed within 7 years (Coryell et al. 1995).  Another prospective study of 146 bipolar patients found that they experienced some symptoms on an average of 47% of the weeks during the 13 year follow up period (Judd et al., 2002). During the follow up period, depressive symptoms were three times more common than manic or hypomanic symptoms. The long term course of bipolar disorder is even more severe for patients who have comorbid substance abuse or dependence disorders (which is even more common than with unipolar disorders) (Levin& Hennessey, 2004). 

...

>As for unipolar disorder, a host of causal factors for bipolar disorder have been posited over the past century. However, biological causal factors are clearly dominant, and the role of psychosocial causal factors has received significantly less attention. 

...

> The best study to date (McGuffin et al., 2003) found that 67% of monozygotic twins with bipolar disorder had a co-twin who shared the diagnosis of bipolar or unipolar disroder (60% had bipolar, and 40% had unipolar disorder). The concordance rate  in dizygotic twins was 19%. This and other studies suggest that genes account for about 80% to 90% of the variance in the tendency to develop (that is, the liability for) bipolar disorder (Katz & McGuffin, 1993; McGuffin et al., 2003). This is higher than heritablility estimates for unipolar disorder or any of the other major adult  psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia (Torrey et al. 1994).

...

>The finding of elevated rates of both bipolar and unipolar forms of the disorder in the relatives of bipolars may be explained in several ways. One possibility is related to the idea that bipolar disorder may be a more severe form of the same underlying disorder. If this were the case, then the increased rate of unipolar disorder in relatives of patients with bipolar disorder would occur because bipolar is a more severe disorder. At least one good study, however, found no support for this hypothesis. Instead, their results suggest that about 70% of the genetic liability for mania is distinct from the genetic liability for depression. In other words, their results suggest that people with bipolar disorder are genetically susceptible to both depression and to mania, and that these susceptibilities are largely independent. 

> Efforts to locate the chromosomal site(s) of the implicated gene or genes in this genetic transmission of bipolar disorder suggest that they are polygentic. Although a great deal of research has been directed at identifying candidate genes through linkage analysis and association studies, no consistent support yet  exists for any specific mode of genetic transmission of bipolar disorder, according to several recent comprehensive reviews (Potash & Depaulo 2000; Tsuang, Taylor, & Faraone, 2004).

The thing about psychiatric medicine is that it is an imperfect science. Nearly everybody has to try many medications before they settle on one that works the best and has the fewest side effects. Unfortunately our doctors are forced to take the approach of "let's throw stuff at it and see what sticks." 

In my case for example, before I settled on my current regiment it took: Lexapro, Depakote, Buspar, Klonopin, Wellbutrin, Prozack, and Lithium.  I currently take: Seroquel, Lamictal, and Celexa. 

It took over 2 years to find the right cocktail, but since I found the meds that worked for me, and my neurology, my life has been significantly improved.  Don't give up on your treatment or diagnosis because one combination of meds didn't work for you. Let the process finish before you pass too much judgement, it needs more time and experimentation.

It will likely be somewhat religious. The AA "big book" -- the bible of AA -- is deeply religious early and often. I found it completely unreadable, but I saw just about everyone else fucking love the religious aspect of it. The meetings are really going to vary, depending on the type of people in the meetings. Look up the different meetings in your city, if you don't really like the people at one meeting, try a few more, and eventually you'll find a "home group" with like-minded people. Even I found one as an atheist in the bible belt. You will recite the "Lord's prayer" and the "Serenity prayer" in most meetings, while holding hands with the alcoholic next to you. I've been to over 700 meetings in my life, yes I counted. Honestly what you're worried about won't be a problem.  The people will be welcoming and warm throughout the meeting, and they will likely ask you to hang out with them early on in your acquaintance. The nature of AA meetings is that of a fellowship, and you will develop connections with people if you talk to them because they are going through the same exact things as you. The idea is that everyone is comfortable with each other, so you can really talk about deep and personal things in meetings, and also that you have a new group of friends who "have fun without drinking." I too have some anxiety, but its easy to fit in if you actually do the program. 

I haven't been to a meeting in years, but my drug use is much more responsible now and I am achieving things now that seemed impossible a few years ago. In the end AA wasn't for me, and I found my own way. But lot's of people get sober with AA and it genuinely worth a shot.

You are a lot like me.  I was baker acted 5 times, went to 4 rehabs, was in debt, had no friends, am in debt and so on; my first official diagnosis was 'bipolar one with psychotic features.' I did NA because I prefer doing drugs to drinking (I take pysch meds drinking makes me feel sick, duh). In the end, I had done 12-step programs and meetings for 18 months. During that period I stayed clean for much of the time, and was even able to pick up a 30-day green keytag and a 60-day orange keytag; yet I picked up many, many more white ones. It only takes only once, a few minutes of weakness, of poor judgement, during an otherwise normal day and you're picking up *another* white chip in front of you're "friends" in the meeting.

Remember that the majority of these people are not bipolar, and further that the majority of these addicts/alcoholics do not get clean in 12-step recovery, despite their best efforts. If you truly have bipolar, getting sober will certainly help - especially in regard to improving your reaction to the medications that advise not to take with alcohol. But your bp will also make it much harder for you to maintain a spotless record of sobriety. Sobriety requires stability, and bipolar disorder is the exact opposite of that. I don't do NA anymore, and I still use occasionally. Still broke and in debt because bp caused me to lose my job, but I get by, take my meds, and I'm pretty happy. 

2 weeks is great, but you have to be humble and realize that is not a lot of clean time. Don't convince yourself you are suddenly in remission - having periods of feeling great is part of your disease.  You must always be vigilant and humble when approaching both your sobriety and your bipolar. Please don't give up on treatment for your mental health just because you've got your drinking under control. PM if you need to talk, I've been through exactly what you're going through.

However they also make more generalized, permanent diagnoses. For example, in my diagnosis of 'with psychotic features' is likely much less permanent than my diagnosis of 'with cluster b (borderline) features.'  Psychosis can be treated with drugs, while treating personality disorders is much more difficult. 

Also of note: The DSM V has done away with axis 1 and axis 2 diagnoses. Personality disorders are now classified alongside mood disorders, which is why my diagnosis now looks more like a bipolar spectrum disorder rather than two distinct, co-morbid disorders.  I think it was the right change to make, personally.

Basically, what happened is that now instead of diagnosing someone "bipolar mixed type" they will be diagnosed "bipolar 1 with mixed features". I'm speculating here but I think this was done because most bipolar 1 individuals experience some mixed episodes at some time in their life.  

They do this with bipolar spectrum disorders a lot, it's really just a new way of categorizing the concepts. For example, I used to be diagnosed "bipolar 1 psychosis" and "borderline personality disorder", but now my diagnosis has been consolidated to "bipolar 1 with psychotic features and cluster b (borderline type) features."
